source.title: VASCULAR COMPLICATIONS IN PEDIATRIC PANCREATITIS: A CASE SERIES

atoms.canonical_statement: The study used the INSPPIRE cohort to describe the frequency, risk factors, and outcomes of peripancreatic vascular complications in children with acute recurrent pancreatitis or chronic pancreatitis.
Eligible participants were children aged 19 years or younger with acute recurrent pancreatitis or chronic pancreatitis enrolled at participating INSPPIRE centers using the study diagnostic criteria.

population.label: Children with ARP or CP enrolled in INSPPIRE
inclusion_criteria: Acute recurrent pancreatitis or chronic pancreatitis by study criteria

atoms.canonical_statement: Splenic, portal, and mesenteric thrombosis and arterial pseudoaneurysm were identified by review of imaging data by pediatric radiologists at each participating site.
Clinical data were collected from March 2012 through February 2017 using standardized patient and physician questionnaires entered into REDCap.
Because INSPPIRE did not record organ-failure duration, the study could not distinguish moderately severe from severe acute pancreatitis and combined these categories.
The primary outcome was recanalization of thrombosis with or without anticoagulant use.

outcome.definition: Recanalization with or without anticoagulant use

atoms.canonical_statement: Secondary outcomes were ICU stay, pancreatic necrosis or pseudocyst, organ failure, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and diabetes mellitus among children with vascular complications.

concept.text: Clinical secondary outcomes among vascular-complication cases

outcome.definition: ICU stay, pancreatic necrosis or pseudocyst, organ failure, EPI, and/or diabetes mellitus

atoms.canonical_statement: The INSPPIRE cohort included 441 children; 58% had acute recurrent pancreatitis and 42% had chronic pancreatitis.

Among 441 children, 349 (about 79%) had more than one acute-pancreatitis episode, totaling 972 attacks; 92 children meeting chronic-pancreatitis criteria reported one or no previous acute-pancreatitis attack.
Across reported acute-pancreatitis attacks, 70.5% were mild, 1.5% were moderately severe or severe, and severity was unknown for 28%.

At least one imaging study was recorded for 410 of 441 children; the database recorded 645 MRI/MRCP studies, 313 CT studies, and 97 follow-up transabdominal ultrasounds, while baseline ultrasound results were not collected.
Peripancreatic vascular complications were identified in 5 of 410 children who had at least one recorded imaging study (1.2%).

population.label: INSPPIRE children with at least one recorded imaging study

concept.text: At least one diagnostic imaging study during INSPPIRE follow-up

atoms.canonical_statement: Among the 5 children with vascular complications, 2 had acute recurrent pancreatitis and 3 had chronic pancreatitis.
Four of the 5 vascular complications occurred during a moderately severe or severe acute-pancreatitis episode; one occurred during mild acute pancreatitis.

concept.text: Moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis at vascular event

quantitative_result.original_result_text: moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis in 4, mild acute pancreatitis in 1

atoms.canonical_statement: Venous thrombosis occurred in 4 of the 5 children with peripancreatic vascular complications.
One of the 5 children with peripancreatic vascular complications had a left gastric artery pseudoaneurysm.
All 5 children with peripancreatic vascular complications were female.

No child with a vascular complication reported contraceptive use, sickle cell disease, cirrhosis, total parenteral nutrition, cigarette smoking, or prior thrombotic events; two had passive tobacco-smoke exposure, and prothrombotic-disorder screening was not performed.
Hypertriglyceridemia was present in 1 of 5 children with vascular complications (20%).
Hypertriglyceridemia was reported in 22 of 441 children in the full INSPPIRE cohort (about 5%).
Among 2 children with venous thrombosis treated with anticoagulant, 1 achieved recanalization.
Among 2 venous-thrombosis patients who did not receive anticoagulants, 1 recanalized.
No bleeding or systemic adverse effects were reported among the 2 children treated with enoxaparin.
The child with a left gastric artery pseudoaneurysm underwent aneurysmal coiling.

exposures.details: Treatment for left gastric artery pseudoaneurysm

atoms.canonical_statement: None of the 5 children with vascular complications required an ICU stay during the corresponding acute-pancreatitis attack.
Pancreatic necrosis was reported in 0 of 5 children with vascular complications.
Organ failure occurred in 1 of 5 children with vascular complications; that child received enoxaparin and later recanalized.
Pseudocyst was reported in 3 of 5 children with vascular complications.
One child developed new-onset diabetes mellitus 5 years after the vascular event.
A separate child with a vascular complication had preexisting exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and diabetes mellitus.

Patient 1 was female, developed acute recurrent pancreatitis at age 3 and splenic-vein thrombosis at age 13 during mild acute pancreatitis; MRI/MRCP identified the event, and the listed genetic risk factor was PRSS1 R122H.

Patient 2 was female, first had acute pancreatitis at age 12 and portal-vein thrombosis at age 14 with chronic pancreatitis during a moderately severe or severe episode; Doppler ultrasound was used, with genetic and duct-obstruction risk factors including PRSS1 R122C, c.40+13C>T, and CFTR TG11-5T/TG11-7T.

Patient 3 was female, first had acute pancreatitis at age 4 and splenic- plus portal-vein thrombosis at age 9 with acute recurrent pancreatitis during a moderately severe or severe episode; CT identified the event, and the risk factor was listed as idiopathic.

Patient 4 was female, first had acute pancreatitis at age 10 and splenic-vein thrombosis at age 15 with chronic pancreatitis during a moderately severe or severe episode; CT identified the event, with hypertriglyceridemia and a PPARG variant listed.

Patient 5 was female, first had acute pancreatitis at age 3 and a left gastric artery pseudoaneurysm at age 6 with chronic pancreatitis during a moderately severe or severe episode; CT identified the event, and pancreas divisum was listed as the risk factor.

Patient 1 received no anticoagulant and recanalized with formation of varices/collaterals; there was no ICU stay, organ failure, or pancreatic necrosis, but a pseudocyst was present and neither EPI nor diabetes was reported.

Patient 2 received no anticoagulant and did not recanalize; there was no ICU stay, organ failure, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst, EPI, or diabetes, and other treatment included ERCP stone extraction and lateral pancreaticojejunostomy.
Patient 3 received enoxaparin and recanalized; organ failure occurred, but no ICU stay, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst, EPI, or diabetes was reported.
Patient 4 received enoxaparin and did not recanalize; there was no ICU stay, organ failure, or pancreatic necrosis, a pseudocyst was present, and EPI and diabetes were preexisting.

Patient 5 received no anticoagulant; Table 2 states did not re-canalize, with no ICU stay, organ failure, or pancreatic necrosis, a pseudocyst, coiling of the pseudoaneurysm plus ERCP with pancreatic duct sphincterotomy and lateral pancreaticojejunostomy, unknown EPI status, and diabetes mellitus.
The splenic vein was the most commonly involved vessel in the pediatric vascular-complication cases.

The authors concluded that peripancreatic vascular complications were rare in children with acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis and were associated with moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis.
The authors observed an all-female pattern among PSMVT cases and stated that the reason for female preponderance in pediatrics was unknown and required further investigation.

Because two of the five cases had cationic trypsinogen mutations and PRSS1 variants are associated with earlier chronic pancreatitis, the authors proposed that children with PRSS1 variants may be at higher risk for PSMVT.

The authors considered hypertriglyceridemia overrepresented among vascular-complication cases relative to the broader INSPPIRE cohort but stated that the small sample precluded statistical comparison.
Genetic testing was incomplete in the cohort.
The dataset lacked organ-failure duration and therefore could not distinguish moderately severe from severe acute pancreatitis under the later NASPGHAN classification.
Data collection was retrospective.

The INSPPIRE cohort excluded children with only one acute-pancreatitis episode without chronic pancreatitis, limiting inference about vascular complications after an isolated acute-pancreatitis attack.
With only five vascular-complication cases, the study could not determine the preferred imaging modality or whether anticoagulants affect outcomes.
The authors stated that anticoagulants appeared safe for PSMVT during an acute-pancreatitis attack, but their overall benefit and long-term impact require further study.
The study reported NIH/NIDDK support under awards R21 DK096327, U01 DK108334, and R01 DK118752; the INSPPIRE registry was developed with CTSA award 2UL1 TR000442 and REDCap.

Disclosures included Mark Lowe serving on the National Pancreas Association board and receiving royalties from Millipore and UpToDate; Tanja Gonska reporting a Vertex research grant and Cystic Fibrosis Foundation consulting; and Aliye Uc reporting professional roles and Cystic Fibrosis Foundation consulting, while the other authors declared no conflicts.
The manuscript directs readers to the PubMed Central web version for supplementary material.
The What is New box states that the incidence of PSMVT was 1.2% in the pediatric ARP/CP cohort.
Using the source-reported 4 venous thromboses among 410 imaged children, the calculated venous-thrombosis frequency is approximately 0.98%.
